title: Paraguay Ousts Its President, Sudan Accuses Ethiopia, Iran Faces a Winter Gas Crisis
bluf: This edition was rebuilt around what most outlets missed. Paraguay's Senate removed President Santiago Peña 44 to 0 after a bank collapse froze deposits for nearly half the country, putting one of Taiwan's last allies in flux. Sudan formally accused Ethiopia at the UN of hosting RSF drone launches, as Ethiopia's own war reignites on three fronts and an Ebola outbreak in Congo passes 10,700 cases with spread to Kenya and Nigeria. In the Gulf, Iran faces a winter gas shortfall and is executing protesters while it negotiates, the Houthis are licensing Red Sea shipping by email, and Gulf fertilizer and sulphur exports are down about 70%, a food and metals shock that will hit after the oil headlines fade. In Washington, Stephen Miller becomes chief of staff Monday and a judge threw out the DOJ suit against Alaska's Senate certification.

corrections.text: Edition 002 said a former FBI agent named Andrew Reyes was charged on November 5. No source could be found for that charge or name. Treat it as unverified; it has been dropped.
Edition 002 gave Scott Colom's Mississippi lead as about 138 votes. The latest count found (Mississippi Free Press) is 43.
Editions 002 and the first version of 003 called the DOJ suit over Alaska's ballots a live certification risk. Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed it on November 1 for lack of standing.
This edition was rebuilt at 8am after the first version repeated mainstream stories. The research now runs through eight parallel regional researchers.

worldConditions.overall: The Iran war and the shipping fight in Hormuz remain the main driver of global risk, with diplomacy and strikes running at the same time. A second front of pressure is building around Taiwan as the PLA's drill season starts. In the US, the transition to a Democratic Congress is orderly but one Senate seat is still in play.
worldConditions.postureBasis: Active US and Iranian kinetic exchanges near a global chokepoint, a major power naval surge near Taiwan, and no ceasefire in Ukraine.

items.headline: Stephen Miller becomes White House chief of staff after the midterm loss
items.summary: Trump named Stephen Miller chief of staff starting November 9, replacing Susie Wiles. Trump frames it as Wiles moving to his political operation; ZeroHedge highlights a claim on Joe Rogan's show that her office signed off on nearly every major decision.
items.assessment: Miller runs immigration policy and is the most ideological figure in the inner circle. Reason argues it will reinforce Trump's worst instincts; supporters see a loyal enforcer for a two year fight with a Democratic Congress.

items.headline: Judge throws out DOJ suit to hold up Alaska's Senate certification
items.summary: Judge Sharon Gleason ruled DOJ lacked standing in United States v. Alaska. DOJ wanted ballots set aside while it checked whether votes for a second 'Daniel J. Sullivan' were meant for Sen. Dan Sullivan. She found ballots already mixed and impossible to separate without breaking ballot secrecy.
items.assessment: The reasoning, that ballot secrecy defeats any remedy, is a ready template for courts facing other postelection suits.

items.headline: DOJ reportedly opens a grand jury probe into the Dobbs leak
items.summary: The DC US Attorney's office under Jeanine Pirro is reportedly subpoenaing people who worked at the Supreme Court in 2022. The Court's own 2023 inquiry never found the leaker. The report builds on a November 5 New York Times story with anonymous sources.
items.assessment: Subpoenas to former clerks would set up a separation of powers fight between the executive and the judiciary, timed right after the midterms.

items.headline: A 181 page progressive memo tells Democrats to subpoena CEOs, not just the White House
items.summary: The Groundwork Collaborative wants hearings with landlords on junk fees, sports betting apps on addiction, grocers on surveillance pricing and AI firms. Rep. Greg Casar wants AI CEOs first; the centrist Progressive Policy Institute is pushing back.
items.assessment: How Democrats split oversight between Trump and corporate America will decide which industries pour money into lobbying in 2027.

items.headline: Wealth taxes lose in California but move forward in Washington and Colorado
items.summary: California's one time 5% billionaire tax was trailing about 56 to 44, and a measure banning such taxes was winning. Repeal of Washington's 9.9% tax on income over $1 million was failing; a Colorado millionaire surtax was narrowly ahead.
items.assessment: The real tax the rich fight is happening in state ballot design, not Congress. Counts were partial.

items.headline: Voters rejected data centers in 38 of 40 plus local races
items.summary: Six cities banned data centers outright and 12 capped their power draw. Mayors who backed hyperscale projects lost in Yukon, Oklahoma (a recall) and Burgin, Kentucky.
items.assessment: Local zoning, not Washington, is becoming the choke point for the AI buildout, a story national outlets barely touched.

items.headline: DC's socialist mayor elect walks into a federal collision
items.summary: Janeese Lewis George will run a city where Congress can veto laws and approve the budget, the National Guard is deployed and there is a $1.1 billion gap. The ACLU of DC wants a local law letting residents sue federal officers who violate their rights.
items.assessment: DC is where a federal takeover and a local left turn meet head on; a local right to sue federal agents would almost certainly end up in court.

alsoNoted.headline: Majority Democrats, a billionaire backed donor group, barred Lever reporters from its Colorado conclave with Buttigieg, Booker and Slotkin
alsoNoted.note: The Lever is a party to the story

alsoNoted.headline: Mississippi Senate still uncalled; affidavit ballots counted from November 10 in Harrison County

items.headline: Iran hangs two Isfahan protesters; two more death sentences in Mashhad
items.summary: Amirhossein Maleki and Amirhossein Ebrahimi, sentenced over the January protests, were hanged. A single source told Iran International that Maleki went through a staged hanging after retracting his confession. Iran Human Rights counts at least 36 protesters executed since March.
items.assessment: Executions are running alongside talks with Washington, a signal that Tehran will not soften at home while bargaining abroad.

items.headline: Gas rich Iran faces a winter shortage and leans on Russia
items.summary: The national gas company says about 130 million cubic meters a day, roughly 16% of last year's output, is still offline after the March strikes. About 11 provinces could face shortages.
items.assessment: Winter gas gaps in Iran mean blackouts and factory shutdowns, a stability risk after January's uprising, and they hand Moscow leverage over Tehran's war and peace choices.

items.headline: Hardliners float leaving the nuclear treaty; the atomic chief attacks the IAEA head
items.summary: After the US midterms, hardline commentators say a Democratic Congress changes nothing and propose threatening to leave the NPT; Hamshahri printed a map of US bases in Europe. Atomic energy chief Mohammad Eslami called IAEA head Rafael Grossi an agent of Iran's enemies.
items.assessment: Eslami's attack lays groundwork to limit inspections whether or not Iran formally leaves the treaty.

items.headline: Kurdish government splits: PUK quits after KDP seats a speaker without it
items.summary: Kurdistan's parliament met for the first time in almost two years and elected KDP's Vala Farid speaker with the PUK boycotting. PUK leader Bafel Talabani says if the KDP appoints regional leaders alone, the PUK will appoint its own in Sulaymaniyah.
items.assessment: That would revive the two administration split of before 2006, with a PUK zone on the Iran border friendlier to Tehran.

items.headline: US reportedly threatens to label Iraq a state sponsor of terrorism over militia weapons
items.summary: Unnamed sources say the US chargé told Baghdad it could face sanctions and the label without a concrete plan to bring militia weapons under state control by June 30, 2027. The militias' conditions include US and Turkish troops leaving and the Kurdish Peshmerga being dissolved.
items.assessment: For a country whose oil money moves through US dollar channels, that label would be a financial chokehold, not a symbol.

items.headline: The Houthis are issuing Red Sea transit permits by email
items.summary: Since declaring a blockade of Saudi Arabia, the Houthis have answered ships' emailed requests for safe passage, usually within 24 hours, per a WSJ investigation. One Chinese container ship got a seven day permit and an offer of Houthi alerts.
items.assessment: A group the US designates as terrorist now runs a working licensing system; every shipowner who asks has a sanctions problem.

items.headline: Aramco profit up 34.6% as it plans a bigger Hormuz bypass pipeline
items.summary: Aramco's third quarter net profit rose to $36.2 billion, and the CEO said engineering has begun to expand the East West pipeline to the Red Sea from 7 to 10 million barrels a day.
items.assessment: The bypass ends exactly where the Houthis now claim to control Saudi shipping, so it trades one chokepoint for another.

items.headline: Saudi Arabia signs a defense pact and $403 million in deals with Syria
items.summary: After Ahmed al Sharaa's second Riyadh trip in a month, the Saudis funded health centers, 10,000 home repairs, water systems and Aleppo's power plant, and the defense ministries signed a cooperation agreement.
items.assessment: Turkey has been Damascus's military patron; Riyadh is buying influence over the new Syrian army, including in Aleppo, Ankara's sphere.

items.headline: Documents tie Press TV's London office to the Sovereign Media network
items.summary: Correspondence shows Press TV London paid Ahmed Kaballo about £41,700, partly in cash via the embassy. Kaballo founded African Stream, which the State Department says RT secretly ran, and now leads Sovereign, which reuses Press TV content and contributors.
items.assessment: No evidence of editorial orders, so this is a gray network; shared contributors and recycled content are better tells than ownership records.

alsoNoted.headline: Iraq's nuclear regulator says fallout from a strike on Iran's Pickaxe Mountain site would barely reach Iraq
Three PMF militia members stopped near Baghdad with 35 rockets (single source)
Iraqi intelligence helped the UAE seize 200,000 Captagon pills
Houthi media claims Saudi strikes killed 11 in Sanaa province (claim)
Epoch Times: Trump says new minor US strikes on Iran; Iran says it downed an MQ-9

items.headline: Hebron siege lifted after election week as October set a record for settler attacks
items.summary: The army withdrew from Hebron on November 2 after a closure that displaced about 5,000 people; the governor puts losses at 10 to 12 million shekels a day in a city that makes about 40% of Palestinian industrial output. OCHA counted 397 damaging settler attacks in 26 days of October, the most since 2006.
items.assessment: The Jerusalem Post reported the army chief advised leaving before the vote and Netanyahu refused, pointing to an electoral motive; closing the industrial hub during the olive harvest drains the Palestinian Authority's tax base.

alsoNoted.headline: Israel burned homes in Haddatha, south Lebanon, despite the June framework; Lebanon counts nearly 4,400 killed since March 2
Opposition still backing Gadi Eisenkot; Herzog names a candidate by November 11

items.headline: Egypt's army uses armed drones on gold miners at the Sudan border, arrests 691
items.summary: The army says it arrested 151 Egyptians and 540 foreigners and confirmed using armed drones; a rights group blames an October air strike on a border mine that killed at least 72 miners.
items.assessment: Cairo is militarizing the gold frontier that feeds RSF smuggling while backing Sudan's army, a quiet Egyptian combat role on the edge of Sudan's war.

items.headline: The Kyiv 'torture house' clash: part real grievance, part influence op
items.summary: About 200 people stormed a National Guard transit house near Kyiv holding mobilized men and deserters; officers used tear gas and warning shots. The woman who set it off posing as a medic was a cosmetologist and has been detained.
items.assessment: Within hours AfD's Alice Weidel was spreading the images, the uproar buried coverage of a Russian strike that killed about 40, and a hijacked air raid app had sent fake radiation alerts the day before. Fake trigger, livestream, Western amplification: a pattern worth recognizing.

items.headline: Ukraine's anticorruption bureau closes the Midas probe; an SBU official threatened a gun during searches
items.summary: NABU finished its investigation into the Mindich energy kickback scheme, alleging 10 to 15% skimmed from Energoatom contracts and over $111 million laundered. In another case NABU says a senior SBU official obstructed searches and threatened to use a firearm; SBU special forces showed up and the acting SBU chief fired two officials.
items.assessment: The armed standoff between agencies is the bigger story: a proxy fight over the President's Office, now run by Kyrylo Budanov, days before Abu Dhabi.

items.headline: Putin ratifies a deal letting bailiffs pull bank data on Russians abroad
items.summary: Russian bailiffs can now ask Kazakhstan, Belarus, Azerbaijan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan where a debtor lives, works and banks, without notifying them.
items.assessment: Exiled journalists often carry politically motivated fines, so this becomes a legal way to map their income and donors in the main relocation hubs.

items.headline: Drone force recruiters found at 49 of Russia's top 50 universities
items.summary: Novaya Gazeta Europe and Molniya found recruiting at 228 universities in 79 regions; students with poor grades face shortened retake deadlines and threats of expulsion followed by conscription.
items.assessment: A quiet mobilization of the educated young the Kremlin claimed to shield, done through academic pressure instead of decrees.

items.headline: St Petersburg cuts its army sign up bonus nearly ninefold
items.summary: The city cut its bonus from 3.5 million rubles to 400,000, its second cut in two weeks; Mari El and Mordovia did the same, and the defense ministry proposed pushing December pay into January.
items.assessment: The cash for recruits model that let Moscow avoid open mobilization is cracking at the regional level.

items.headline: Inside Kiriyenko's propagandist training pipeline
items.summary: The 'New Media Workshop', run through sanctioned Dialog Regiony and linked to the Doppelgänger operation, claims 1,700 graduates staffing RT, Solovyov Live and outlets in occupied Ukraine.
items.assessment: Moscow's own internet throttling backfires: pro government Telegram views fell 41% against 16.5% for opposition channels.

items.headline: Kremlin source: Putin saw the Finnish and Norwegian call as an opening to Europe
items.summary: Per Farida Rustamova's Vlast newsletter, Putin views Finland and Norway as softer than Berlin, Paris and London; both want a standing channel, and Kyiv coordinated the October 26 call.
items.assessment: Moscow is trying to make the Nordics its preferred European interlocutors and sideline the big three.

items.headline: Armenia's opposition unites after billionaire Karapetyan's arrest
items.summary: The Russian Armenian billionaire and 35 associates were jailed; hours later opposition groups formed an alliance against constitutional changes Baku demands before signing the peace treaty.
items.assessment: Pashinyan lacks the two thirds needed for a referendum, so snap elections are likely, and Moscow's best placed proxy is in jail.

items.headline: Georgia's ruling party moves to limit election challenges; Russia bans a pro European party
items.summary: Watchdogs warn a Georgian Dream bill limits challenges to final results to technical errors and scraps random recounts. The same day Russia declared the opposition party Droa undesirable.
items.assessment: Domestic restrictions and Moscow's labels reinforce each other against Georgia's strongest pro European critics.

alsoNoted.headline: Draft Russian central bank rules would give the FSB automatic surveillance of crypto exchange customers
Japan Tobacco's seized Russian plants reportedly handed to Putin associate Timur Bolloev
Helsinki court jails the Fitburg's Russian captain and Azerbaijani boatswain for dragging an anchor over Baltic cables
Poland's Constitutional Tribunal crisis (October 30): see Alternative Media for Craig Murray's account; mainstream follow up not collected

sections.quietNote: Thin this run: the Europe researcher ran out of search budget. Poland's Tribunal crisis is the biggest gap.

items.headline: US licenses Hungary's MOL to start taking Serbia's NIS refinery from Russia
items.summary: OFAC allowed MOL initial steps, transfer of Russian origin securities and Russian approvals, but not closing; Budapest expects a deal by December 11.
items.assessment: Serbia's energy exit from Russia is being brokered by Budapest, while a new student led government takes over in Belgrade.

alsoNoted.headline: Hungary halts its subsidy program for Republika Srpska
Hungarian Conservative: Serbia's student list will be tougher on Kosovo than Vučić

items.headline: China's top military command is down to two men after the plenum purge
items.summary: After the Fifth Plenum expelled 33 members, 16 of them military, only Xi Jinping and Zhang Shengmin hold seats on the seven seat Central Military Commission. The plenum also told provincial bosses to speak last in meetings and curbed demands for personal loyalty; retired General Wang Ning was removed from the top advisory body November 5.
items.assessment: A commission this empty puts command authority in Xi's hands personally, which cuts against claims the PLA is war ready. Read it next to the Taiwan air surge: loud signaling, hollow top.

items.headline: Beijing passes a cross border anticorruption law with global reach
items.summary: The NPC Standing Committee passed a law giving Beijing new tools to chase offshore assets; earlier drafts also aimed to counter foreign corruption probes of Chinese firms.
items.assessment: It builds a legal basis for seizing assets and pressuring diaspora businesspeople abroad, extending Chinese jurisdiction past its borders.

items.headline: A Wuhan court is hearing a $53.5 billion Covid 'defamation' suit against Missouri
items.summary: Chinese authorities and research institutes sued the US state of Missouri over Covid claims, and hearings began.
items.assessment: Mirror lawfare: a counter judgment against Missouri's earlier multibillion dollar default ruling against China, built to deter seizure of Chinese assets.

items.headline: China's central bank brakes the yuan with its first FX reserve hike in five years
items.summary: Banks' foreign currency reserve requirement rises from 4% to 6% on November 15, locking up an estimated $20 to 25 billion. The yuan had risen 14 sessions straight; it then fell to a two week low.
items.assessment: Beijing is choosing exporters over a strong currency just as a record trade surplus looms, which will feed the overcapacity backlash (see Thailand's EV tax).

alsoNoted.headline: Ex Politburo member Ma Xingrui indicted on bribery going back to the late 1990s
Rare earth export control suspension expires November 10; Beijing kept its licensing system in place

items.headline: New Zealand votes today with a 6% party holding the balance
items.summary: The final 1News Verian poll had National 30, Labour 29, Greens 16, ACT 10, NZ First 8 and the Opportunity party 6.2, leaving both blocs short of 61 seats. Unemployment hit 5.7%, an 11 year high.
items.assessment: With both big parties near 30 year lows, government could hinge on overhang seats and special votes; expect days of uncertainty and leverage shifting to a party that has never been in coalition.

items.headline: Indonesia busts a ring trafficking its citizens into Russia's army
items.summary: Police arrested 13 suspects, including two Russians and a Ukrainian, with 58 alleged victims recruited through TikTok and Facebook ads and sent on tourist visas. Jakarta formally asked Moscow to stop recruiting Indonesians.
items.assessment: Russia's manpower pipeline has reached the largest Muslim country, and a nonaligned partner is pushing back publicly; a Ukrainian suspect suggests a commercial network, not only a state one.

items.headline: North Korea rehearses knocking out allied airbases, with doctored photos
items.summary: KCNA reported anti aircraft missile tests and a cruise missile dropping cluster munitions on a mock runway; NK News found the images heavily manipulated. Border loudspeakers are installed but silent.
items.assessment: Read it as a rehearsal for a first strike on US and South Korean airpower, but discount capability claims given the doctoring.

items.headline: Pyongyang's quiet diplomatic thaw before APEC
items.summary: Kim Jong Un's international department chief went to Beijing ten days after Kim visited Dandong; Brazil's first ambassador in a decade took up his post. Kim Yo Jong said talks with the US are possible but not necessary and rejected the FBI's attribution of the $6.3 billion Binance theft.
items.assessment: Pyongyang is building normal diplomatic standing with Global South and Russia aligned states so it can negotiate from recognition.

items.headline: Thailand triples tax on imported EVs as Chinese competition bites
items.summary: The cabinet raised excise on imported battery EVs from 10% to 35% starting January to protect local manufacturing.
items.assessment: A friendly ASEAN state is now erecting barriers to Chinese EVs, pushing BYD and others to build locally instead of exporting.
items.source: Reuters via China Global South Project

alsoNoted.headline: Airstrikes reportedly killed 16 in Myanmar as the ASEAN envoy arrived; China reopened trade at crossings held by armed groups
Nikkei fell 4.4% and Kospi 3.3% on fears a Democratic Congress scrutinizes AI data centers

items.headline: Pakistan's ousted provincial chief is still missing as the coalition cracks
items.summary: Since emergency rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on October 11, former chief minister Sohail Afridi and two PTI lawmakers are in 'protective custody' and 200 plus public order cases were filed. Coalition partner Bilawal Bhutto told the government to stop fighting everyone; JUI-F protested alleged drone surveillance of Fazlur Rehman's home.
items.assessment: The state is now fighting PTI, JUI-F, Kabul and India at once while Iran war costs squeeze the economy; expect louder dissent from inside the coalition.

alsoNoted.headline: Pakistan struck Taliban posts at Angoor Adda; Rubio backed Islamabad

items.headline: Havana reportedly met US officials in New York the day its foreign minister denied talks
items.summary: Martí Noticias, citing anonymous sources, reports Vice Minister Carlos Fernández de Cossío led an unannounced meeting with US officials during the UN General Assembly on September 24, the same day Bruno Rodríguez told AP no meetings were planned.
items.assessment: With Democrats taking Congress, Havana has reason to keep quiet channels open while waiting Washington out. Martí is US government media, so weigh the sourcing.

items.headline: Barbados PM: Cuba needs food and power before talk of political change
items.summary: Mia Mottley told CNN Cuba must first secure food and energy, and this time did not blame the embargo.
items.assessment: A Caribbean ally of Havana shifting tone is a small but telling crack in regional cover for the government.

alsoNoted.headline: Treasury sanctions a brother of the late López-Calleja and the daughter of GAESA chief Ania Lastres; four Freemasons sentenced
CFR: Cuba has lost 13 to 25% of its population since 2020; fewest births since 1899
alsoNoted.note: September piece, still the best data

sections.quietNote: No new Brazil items verified this run; the Latin America researcher ran out of search budget before reaching Brazil.

items.headline: Paraguay's Senate removes President Santiago Peña, who is detained at home
items.summary: The Senate voted 44 to 0 to remove Peña for poor performance after the central bank took over Ueno Bank, freezing deposits for about 3 million clients, close to half the country. Prosecutors accuse him of favoring a bank he had business ties to, including with public pension money. Vice President Pedro Alliana serves until 2028.
items.assessment: Paraguay is one of Taiwan's last diplomatic allies and Peña was a close Milei and Trump partner; a sudden handover is a moment Beijing and Washington will both test.

items.headline: Venezuela bombs an ELN camp, breaking 20 years of chavista tolerance
items.summary: Government drones hit an ELN guerrilla camp in Apure, apparently with a cocaine lab, killing at least 19; the NYT reported US help.
items.assessment: InSight Crime thinks Venezuela's forces would lose a long fight with the ELN, so expect a joint push with Washington and Colombia, and ELN reprisals against officials who once profited from it.

items.headline: Machado and González back a US plan: new courts first, elections within six months
items.summary: The State Department plan would name new Supreme Court and electoral council members by year end, declare the presidency vacant, then hold a vote within six months, possibly July 24.
items.assessment: Order matters: Jorge Rodríguez's Assembly is already vetting about 260 court applicants, so chavismo shapes the referee before anyone votes.

items.headline: Venezuela's reserves fall despite $90 oil
items.summary: Oikos Research finds prices up 245% since December while the bolívar fell 198%, and the central bank lost a net $608 million in reserves; the budget assumed $55 oil.
items.assessment: Propping the currency with an oil windfall before an election is the 2012 playbook; the bill comes after the vote.

items.headline: Venezuela softens its Hate Law: prison out, dollar fines in
items.summary: A first reading replaces 10 to 20 year sentences with fines of 500 to 10,000 times the dollar rate; press unions want repeal and 140 web domains stay blocked.
items.assessment: Enforcement stays with Diosdado Cabello's Interior Ministry, and dollar priced fines can bankrupt a local outlet as surely as prison.

items.headline: Nicaragua drops Cuban and Venezuelan troops from its 2027 military permits but keeps Russia
items.summary: Decree 13/2026 lists foreign forces allowed in for exercises; for the first time since 2020 Cuba and Venezuela are out, Russia keeps the largest quota.
items.assessment: The ALBA military bloc is quietly unwinding while Moscow's foothold stays.

items.headline: Bukele's 2,000 troops in Haiti operate outside the UN force
items.summary: About 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers with armor and air support deployed after an October ambush; the UN says most sit outside the Gang Suppression Force. A gang boss wrote to the UN seeking a truce.
items.assessment: El Salvador's mano dura model is operating abroad with no UN human rights reporting; its future is decided at a November 16 to 17 meeting.

items.headline: Colombia's forensic institute pushes back on soldiers moving bodies after combat
items.summary: Medicina Legal asked that troops be barred from moving bodies or belongings on their own under a draft decree on deaths in security operations.
items.assessment: Colombia's war crimes court attributes 6,402 civilian killings dressed up as combat deaths to the army; control of the scene was how they were hidden.

items.headline: Mexico's election authority files a criminal complaint after its chair quits
items.summary: The INE asked prosecutors to investigate former chair Guadalupe Taddei, who resigned over ties to a contractor; about 30 senior staff have left and all contracts, including voter ID production, are under review.
items.assessment: A weakened referee going into the 2027 midterms hands the governing coalition leverage over its next leaders.

alsoNoted.headline: IPYS: 17.7 million Venezuelans live in local news deserts; 96% of surveyed journalists self censor
An unsealed 1983 oil well in Salta, Argentina has leaked for three years, killing 20 hectares of forest
OAS sets 30, 60 and 90 day deadlines for Nicaragua on political prisoners and elections

items.headline: The AI fake ID kingpin is free and explains how he beat bank checks
items.summary: Yuriy Nazarenko's OnlyFake sold more than 10,000 AI generated IDs at about $15 each, used by North Korean fake IT workers; he pleaded guilty, served about a year and left the US.
items.assessment: Know your customer checks at banks and fintechs fell to a $15 tool, and copycats are still running.

alsoNoted.headline: Meta paused terms letting it train AI on business website content after a Norwegian injunction and a UK probe

items.headline: ICE moving to deport up to 80 Afghans, including people who aided US forces
items.summary: The Free Press profiles a former Kabul police officer who worked with US troops, now held in Louisiana; 66 Democratic lawmakers asked Rubio to cancel the flights, reportedly routed through Pakistan.
items.assessment: Criticism from a center right outlet shows the issue cuts across party lines.

sections.quietNote: See the reported US threat to label Iraq a terror sponsor and Somalia's crisis.

items.headline: Sudan takes Ethiopia to the UN Security Council over RSF drones launched from Ethiopian soil
items.summary: Khartoum cites 70 attacks with 187 one way drones from February to October, 28 in October alone, killing 176 soldiers; it names Asosa airport, the Kurmuk border area and Bahir Dar airbase as launch sites. Addis says Sudan's army backs TPLF linked rebels.
items.assessment: Sudan's war and Ethiopia's new war are merging into one proxy system; Egypt and Sudan reaffirmed Nile claims against Ethiopia on November 2, hardening a Cairo and Khartoum bloc against a UAE backed Addis.

items.headline: Ethiopia's old enemies now fight together: Fano cuts the A2 highway
items.summary: Amhara Fano fighters reportedly took Ibnat and cut parts of the A2 between Dessie and Woldia, Addis Ababa's supply line north, while federal forces push toward Sheraro in Tigray. TPLF and Fano leaders released a joint video vowing to overthrow the government.
items.assessment: Enemies from the 2020 to 2022 war now operate as one alliance; most battlefield claims are unverified.

items.headline: Fighting over Moyale pushes about 50,000 people into Kenya; grenades hit a Kenyan school
items.summary: Ethiopian Somalis and Oromos have fought over Moyale since October 18; on November 1 three RPGs fired from Ethiopia hit a primary school in Kenyan Moyale.
items.assessment: A third Ethiopian front, separate from Tigray and Amhara, now strains Kenya, a key US security partner.

items.headline: Somalia's Supreme Court strikes down the president's term extension a day after he fired the chief justice
items.summary: The court ruled Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's one year extension unlawful and that his term ended in May; he had dismissed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed the night before. Uganda will pull all its troops out at the end of next year.
items.assessment: A legitimacy crisis just as donors cut mission funding and the largest troop contributor leaves favors al Shabaab; watch the Gulf and Turkish patrons.

items.headline: Nigerian court voids Atiku's opposition nomination ten weeks before the vote
items.summary: The Federal High Court threw out the ADC leadership under David Mark, and Atiku Abubakar's nomination fell with it; the ADC will appeal and blames the ruling APC, which denies a role.
items.assessment: If it stands, the January 16 race has no major northern candidate, risky for a north already hit by insurgency; this is lawfare, not open repression.

items.headline: Guinea expels more than 8,000 Burkinabè gold miners

angles.title: The Iran war's hidden food and metals shock is sulphur, not oil
angles.argument: Gulf fertilizer exports fell about 70% (994,000 tonnes in September against 3.41 million a year earlier). The Gulf supplies 30 to 40% of seaborne urea and up to half of seaborne sulphur.
angles.whyNonObvious: Sulphur becomes sulphuric acid, which phosphate fertilizer plants and copper and nickel leaching both need. So a shipping war can show up months later as higher food prices after the next planting, and as a squeeze on battery metals, long after headlines say the crisis eased.
angles.counter: Rystad says China, Russia, Oman and the US are filling much of the gap, so it is a price problem more than a shortage.

angles.title: Iran is building a paperwork regime for Hormuz that could outlast any ceasefire
angles.argument: October saw 750 Hormuz transits, the most since July, led by bulkers and a record 32 LNG carriers. Iran's new strait authority has blacklisted 240 vessels and threatens fines or seizure.
angles.whyNonObvious: A blacklist and permit system is a sovereignty claim. Even with a peace deal, shipowners may face Iranian compliance demands on top of US sanctions risk, the same trap the Houthis are now creating with emailed Red Sea permits.
angles.counter: The IMO counted 30 attacks in October and still advises against transit; some transit counts are estimates.

angles.title: The world has about 22 ships to fix undersea internet cables, and no wartime plan
angles.outlet: War on the Rocks (Nikolich and Gallo)
angles.argument: Roughly 22 repair ships handle 150 to 200 cable faults a year. The authors want a US coordinator, a government backed repair fleet and spare parts stockpiles.
angles.whyNonObvious: An adversary does not need to cut every cable, only faster than they can be fixed, or scare crews off. The Red Sea, where the Houthis now license shipping, is also a cable chokepoint; a 2024 Houthi strike led to three cuts that took six months to repair.
angles.counter: Route diversity and satellite backup may make cables less of a single point of failure than the authors suggest.

angles.title: Golden Dome could cause the arms race it is meant to stop
angles.outlet: War on the Rocks (Lamb and Grego)
angles.argument: Rivals react to what a funded program might do, so even a weak missile shield drives Russian and Chinese buildups, and New START limits already lapsed in February.
angles.whyNonObvious: A space interceptor would have roughly 25 seconds against a submarine launched missile, which pushes launch authority toward automation. And space interceptors double as satellite killers, inviting a nuclear blast in orbit as the countermove.
angles.counter: Hawks such as Hudson's Michael Doran argue Iran's missile advantage proved defenses are what stabilize.

angles.title: Private AI labs could become veto players in US and China nuclear diplomacy
angles.argument: The proposed US and China AI hotline should stay narrow and start with defining human control in nuclear command systems.
angles.whyNonObvious: US promises are only credible if frontier labs are forced to report AI incidents, so a few companies hold leverage over nuclear diplomacy, just as the AI selloff squeezes them. Flawed AI intelligence reports are a likelier escalation path than an AI deciding to launch.
angles.counter: No AI crisis has forced the issue, and voluntary measures tend to be abandoned.

angles.title: Quantum sensors that can't be jammed may change submarine and mine hunting
angles.outlet: War on the Rocks (Chávez and Yao)
angles.argument: Quantum magnetometers are the most field ready quantum technology: tunnel detection, submarine and mine hunting, navigation without GPS.
angles.whyNonObvious: They emit nothing, so they are hard to detect or jam, and they could undercut ships' magnetic cloaking in shallow seas like the South China Sea. But magnetic navigation depends on maps that are thinnest over enemy territory.
angles.counter: Cluttered chokepoints like Hormuz are the hardest case for these sensors, exactly where mine hunting is needed now.

angles.title: The first US war started without majority public support, and Congress now holds the purse
angles.argument: Democrats can defund, subpoena or pass war powers resolutions; defunding is the strongest tool, but the 2007 Iraq precedent shows leaders folding after a veto.
angles.whyNonObvious: Because the war is mostly naval escort duty at an estimated $2 to 3 billion a month, there is no occupation for opposition to rally around. Israel cuts both ways: critics say it serves an ally, while the White House can shift blame onto Israel.
angles.counter: Paul Poast (Chicago Council) expects Congress to get further on tariffs than on Iran.

angles.title: With munitions short, the blockade, not bombing, is Washington's real lever
angles.argument: After the midterms Washington may think it can wait while the blockade squeezes Iran; Tehran will not accept no war, no peace forever.
angles.whyNonObvious: If renewed strikes look like a low cost way to recover standing after the midterm loss, the timing of escalation may track domestic politics, not the battlefield.
angles.counter: Cole Bucy argues Iran's post decapitation leaders believe only sustained Hormuz pressure keeps them alive, so waiting is risky.

angles.title: The Houthis are getting stronger with time, not weaker
angles.argument: The Houthis hold much of Yemen's Red Sea coast, have a unified command against fractured rivals, and a new ceasefire would mostly let them rearm.
angles.whyNonObvious: Controlling the state lets them conscript and indoctrinate children, so time works for them demographically even with thin popular support.
angles.counter: Bab al Mandab transits actually rose in October (1,196), per S&P.

angles.title: Wars now end in pauses, not peace, and that matters for Abu Dhabi
angles.outlet: War on the Rocks (Dafna Rand, Gideon Rose)
angles.argument: Modern wars end in on again, off again pauses; outside powers keep losing sides fighting.
angles.whyNonObvious: US leverage over its own partners shrinks the longer a war runs, so in Abu Dhabi the hard gap may be between Kyiv's and its backers' definitions of victory, not the map.
angles.counter: Some argue the Iran campaign shows decisive results are still possible.
